title: Oldest male orca on record may have been identified thanks to historical atomic bomb testing
summary: Researchers might have identified the oldest male orca ever recorded after testing for radioactive traces of atomic bombs in the teeth of whales stranded in Scotland.
body: Nuclear fallout has potentially revealed the oldest male orca ever recorded, scientists have found. The radioactive residue, a result of bomb testing in previous decades, was preserved in the teeth of orcas ( Orcinus orca ) and sperm whales ( Physeter macrocephalus ) that washed up over the years in Scotland, according to a recent study. "It gives us what we call a kind of bomb pulse," study first author Kieran Tierney , a research scientist at the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre, told Live Science. Male orcas are thought to have a maximum lifespan of around 50 to 60 years. However, in the recent study, published Oct. 1 in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science , the radiocarbon signature identified in one stranded male suggested he had lived to more than 65 years old. The research team noted that the radiocarbon data doesn't provide a precise age. However, that doesn't mean the estimate is implausible. Maximum ages are notoriously difficult to measure in nature — researchers can't track every animal to see which individual lives longest in all species — and there isn't an extensive worldwide record of orca longevity. title: 'I would love to discover Attila's grave': Live Science readers weigh in on which archaeological discoveries they would want to find
summary: Live Science asked its readers what type of archaeological find they'd want to discover.
body: From people's backyards to famous excavation sites , archaeological discoveries found the world over give clues about the cultures and lives of ancient peoples. For instance, the discovery of 1,200-year-old pennies in Denmark revealed that the Vikings melted down silver from the Muslim world , while an excavation of a 2,800-year-old tomb with sacrificed horses in Siberia revealed ties to the nomadic Scythians . Other archaeological discoveries are important due to their historical significance or extraordinary preservation. For example, the 40,000-year-old "Lion Man" statuette was carved by humans in what is now Germany during the last ice age, and it may be the earliest known evidence of religious belief in the world. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide clues about mysterious and long-lost languages, such as the Linear A writing system from the ancient Minoans of Crete. Other texts, like the Rosetta stone , helped crack the code of Egyptian hieroglyphics, allowing researchers to better understand this ancient culture. Each type of archaeological discovery unearths something new about the ancient world. This week, Live Science polled its readers on which of these types of finding…

title: 'You had one job': Astrophysicist and Star Trek science advisor Erin MacDonald on the secret to her success and the science flubs that haunt her
summary: Live Science spoke with astrophysicist Erin Macdonald about her role as a science adviser for 'Star Trek' and other Hollywood movies.
body: From gravitational waves to time travel , science has always been at the heart of "Star Trek". While the franchise has never shied away from imagining the impossible, much of its appeal comes from making strange situations seem believable. That's where the role of a science adviser comes in. It's not necessarily about making sure everything is scientifically accurate, but understanding the science well enough to know where creative liberties can be taken and how to make them come alive on screen. Erin Macdonald knows this balance all-too-well. After studying general relativity and gravitational waves for her doctorate and spending years working at Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), Macdonald shifted gears and became a science advisor for six "Star Trek" series, including the "Discovery" franchise, as well as a variety of other television and film projects. Live Science spoke with Macdonald about how she brings the world of "Star Trek" to life, and her job's biggest pitfalls. KHC: How did you end up getting into the field of science advising? title: Earliest monster black hole found at the universe's edge — pushing theories to their limits
summary: Scientists have discovered the earliest-known quasar lurking in the ancient universe — and it's growing at a slower rate than scientists believed possible.
body: A Euclid space telescope image of the newfound quasar (red dot in the center), which is further away than any known active galactic nucleus found yet. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, Wolf et al. 2026) Astronomers have just discovered the earliest-known quasar — and it's 40 million years older than the previous record holder. The finding, which observed the object at just 630 million years after the Big Bang, could help researchers to better understand how black holes developed in the early universe. "Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew," study co-author Julien Wolf , a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, said in a statement . "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both." The object — estimated to have the mass of 360 million suns — was described in a new study published Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics . title: Scientists may have discovered new branch on the human family tree, 100,000-year-old tooth in China suggests
summary: One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.
body: In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage. In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature , researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo " group, the researchers wrote. The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating , the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicusp…

title: Why Nobel physics prize winner Francis Halzen staked his career on an 'almost non-existent piece of reality'
summary: Live Science spoke with Nobel laureate Francis Halzen on how he got into physics "by accident" and built a neutrino detector that changed it forever.
body: When Francis Halzen first proposed burying a $271 million telescope deep beneath the South Pole, he expected to be laughed off stage. Four decades later, it won him a Nobel Prize. Consisting of thousands of light sensors strung like rosary beads inside a cubic kilometer (0.2 cubic miles) of pristine ice, his detector, aptly named IceCube, is not an obvious way to study the universe. But Halzen , a theoretical physicist at the University of Madison-Wisconsin, isn't looking for something obvious. His quarries are neutrinos , near-massless, chargeless, shapeshifters that are the most abundant material particles in existence. They form from nuclear processes and high-energy collisions, swarming out of our sun and whizzing from the outskirts of black holes. Yet though neutrinos stream through stars, planets, and us every second in their trillions, you still have a 75% chance of living your entire life without a single one striking an atom in your body . On the rare occasions neutrinos do interact with atoms, they create charged particles that zip through water or ice faster than light does, casting a faint blue cone — the optical equivalent of a sonic boom . Since 2011, IceCube has bee…

title: It's time to look at Uranus: How to see the solar system's strangest planet at its best this week
summary: On Wednesday (Nov. 25), the distant ice giant Uranus will be at its best and brightest. Here's when, where and how to look for the seventh planet.
body: One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system — the distant ice giant Uranus — reaches its annual opposition on Wednesday (Nov. 25), just a day after the Beaver Supermoon . It's the best time to see the seventh planet from the sun, but you'll need to use stargazing binoculars or a good backyard telescope to find it. Uranus is faint, slow-moving and rarely a target for casual stargazers. However, on Nov. 25, and, for a few weeks on either side, it will be at its closest point to Earth this year and will appear at its brightest, making it possible to spot. Opposition occurs when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun; Uranus will be "opposite" the sun, hence, "opposition." The moment of opposition will happen at 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 25, according to EarthSky . Consequently, Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point in the sky around midnight and set in the west around sunrise. You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters and M45. Uranus will be a few degrees southeast of the cluster, appearing as a faint point of light, about two-fifths of the distance between the Pleiades and Al…

body: Update: On Tuesday (Nov. 24) ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on X that the BepiColombo team has isolated the computer glitch, and tweaked the mission accordingly. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24). After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun. Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team. However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury. ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft…

title: Impossible volcanic eruption spotted in deepest part of the ocean, perplexing scientists
summary: Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.
body: A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity. This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern , a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery. Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79. "It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sun…

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate . title: 2,200-year-old Celtic silver coin hoard unearthed at construction site in Hungary
summary: Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.
body: Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades. Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C. The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said. The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said. During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground. "This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter , an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Instit…

title: Black holes can spin so fast they rip in half 'like pants', study finds
summary: Astrophysicists have dared to ask a cosmological question never asked before: Do black holes "wear pants"? New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.
body: Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle. In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D , researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes . The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes. "Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper. Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales. Do black holes wear pants? title: Scientists find 2 'peculiar' spiral galaxies pulling each other apart
summary: A stunning new image from the Gemini North telescope captures two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity, helping to trigger the birth of new stars.
body: Quick facts What it is: NGC 7253 (also called Arp 278), a pair of interacting spiral galaxies Where it is: 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Pegasus When it was shared: Sept. 1, 2026 Picture a spiral galaxy, and you'll probably imagine a swirl of stars. But some galaxies appear to be the complete opposite. One is NGC 7253, which looks more like a bizarre balloon animal than a cosmic coil. In reality, it's two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. As shown in this recent image from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii, the galaxies' once-ordered shapes are being disturbed and disrupted as their mutual gravitational pull stretches and distorts their spiral arms into a tangled arrangement of stars, gas and dust. It sounds and looks chaotic and destructive, but encounters between galaxies don't mean stars are physically colliding; the distances between individual stars are too great. Instead, something extraordinarily productive can happen. Spiral galaxies contain huge clouds of cold gas and dust, particularly within their arms. title: Which came first: black holes or galaxies?
summary: Astronomers once assumed galaxies were born before black holes, but giant black holes spotted in the early universe are forcing them to rethink their order of events.
body: Nearly every large galaxy is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its center. The Milky Way's black hole, known as Sagittarius A*, is enormous, weighing over 4 million times as much as the sun . But which came first: the black holes or the galaxies around them? Astronomers told Live Science that they thought they knew, but new observations mean they're no longer sure. Challenging the standard model For decades, the prevailing idea was that galaxies came first: Dying massive stars leave behind black holes that can merge and feed until they swell to millions of times the sun's mass, said Joseph Silk , an astrophysicist and professor at Johns Hopkins University. Then, in recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) began peering back at the early universe. "Recent observations are challenging this picture, or at least showing us that it cannot be the whole story," Roberto Maiolino , a professor of astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science in an email. "We are finding extremely massive black holes just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang." The galaxy GHZ2 (white box) contains the oldest known supermassive black hole. title: 'Like walking the plank': For 3,000 years, Indigenous people herded bison off a unique cliff in Texas, study reveals
summary: At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.
body: Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought. "Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity . Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia. title: Meet the science adviser behind Netflix's hit series 'Below'
summary: Live Science spoke with marine biologist Annie Mercier about her role as a science adviser for Netflix's show "Below."
body: In Netflix's new series " Below ," an ancient, squid-like creature known as "Mudder" threatens a small coastal community in Newfoundland, Canada, arriving around the same time as a mysterious iceberg that starts causing dangerous hallucinations in the town's residents. The series blends marine science, horror and environmental themes, harking back to Newfoundland's long-standing connections with giant squid ( Architeuthis dux ), with the first sightings going back to the 1870s . Annie Mercier , a marine biologist in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, was brought on as a science adviser in 2025 just before Netflix began shooting "Below." Mercier's research focuses on deep sea organisms, studying their behavior, interactions and how they respond to environmental stressors like climate change. Mercier's lab at the Ocean Sciences Center was used as a filming location, and she met with actor Mackenzie Davis, who plays the research scientist Dr. Fonda Howander, to guide the character. title: Why do wolves howl?
summary: Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.
body: Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl , but they are most known for their iconic howl. The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place? Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network. Howl you doin'? Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum , a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other." However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said. When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl m…

title: James Webb telescope spots giant star swallowing its companion in first-ever observations of a stellar merger
summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope followed up on years-old observations to confirm the first recorded act of a giant star swallowing its companion. The stellar cannibalism occurred just next door, in the Andromeda galaxy.
body: For the first time, astronomers have caught two stars — a supergiant and a star slightly smaller than the sun — in the act of merging. After orbiting each other for thousands of years, the pair came together in just under seven years — a span short enough that researchers could watch the drama play out from start to finish. The discovery was described in a study published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature . "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," Viraj Karambelkar , an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, said in a NASA statement . "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do." The stars' imminent merger was originally picked up by NASA's now-retired Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer — a spacecraft that was designed to spot asteroids but also discovered many other interesting changes in the night sky . Researchers noticed that a previously stable binary star system in the Andromeda galaxy , the closest major galaxy to ours, had begun to brighten. title: Ghostly 'sand body' double burial unearthed at Sutton Hoo
summary: During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.
body: Archaeologists have discovered a mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo , an Anglo-Saxon cemetery in the U.K. that's famous for an enormous seventh-century ship burial of an early medieval king. The unusual grave does not have any bones but rather ghost-like shapes where a body was once buried. Sand bodies were "burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person, not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii," Angus Wainwright , an archaeologist at the U.K.'s National Trust, said in a statement . These burials have been found at Sutton Hoo in the past, as well as at other Anglo-Saxon sites in the Suffolk area of the U.K. The new sand burial, which was uncovered at a burial ground called Garden Field at the end of a 2025 dig, features in a four-part documentary created by the television series "Time Team" and archaeological experts with the National Trust and FAS Heritage. Whereas a 2024 excavation unearthed pieces of a bronze bucket used in a cremation ritual, the 2025 excavation was aimed at discovering evidence for the extent of the cemetery, when it was used and whether the people buried there were connected …

title: Voyager 1 stops sending science data ahead of its light-day milestone — but NASA has a plan
summary: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft just reached 1 light-day from our planet, but a newfound glitch in the probe's onboard computer is preventing it from sharing science data with Earth.
body: NASA has confirmed that its Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached a record-breaking 1 light-day from Earth — but new milestones come with old problems. On Nov. 14, the Voyager mission team discovered that the nearly 50-year-old space probe had stopped sending science data back to Earth, according to NASA — a problem that the team had to deal with as recently as 2024. As of Thursday (Nov. 19), the team had not resolved the problem. But they did detect a "carrier" signal that is used to ferry science and engineering information from Voyager 1 to Earth, confirming that the probe is still powered up and pointed in the right direction. "We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," Suzanne Dodd , Voyager project manager, said at a NASA news conference Thursday, adding that she is "confident" that the science data will continue flowing again soon. Using the carrier signal, the team confirmed that the probe had reached its latest distance milestone of 1 light-day from Earth, or roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away, Wednesday (Nov. 18). At this distance, which no human-made object had ever reached before, it takes a full 24 hours for radio signals traveling at the speed o…

title: Dinosaur quiz: Can you name these 12 dinosaurs?
summary: Can you name all 12 dinosaurs in this science quiz?
body: Before an asteroid slammed into Earth 66 million years ago, dinosaurs had roamed our planet for more than 160 million years. They emerged around 230 million to 240 million years ago, during the Triassic period, when the supercontinent Pangaea had united the landmasses. As Pangaea broke apart, dinosaurs went on to inhabit continents all over the world, including what became Antarctica, which was a temperate rainforest during the Cretaceous period. Dinosaurs lived in diverse ecosystems, from the snowy Arctic to the hot equatorial regions of Gondwana , a supercontinent in the Southern Hemisphere. As dinosaurs evolved in their different environments, they developed distinct defenses and adaptations to help them survive. Researchers have discovered hundreds upon hundreds of dinosaur species, from the small "dwarf dinosaur" that lived on an island in Transylvania to the hulking, long-necked Dreadnoughtus in Argentina. title: What if space and time don't exist? Physicists are chasing hints that our reality emerges from something deeper
summary: Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.
body: Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence. Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental. But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes , quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper? "You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw , a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science. Two theories that do not fit For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible. In Einstein's general theory of relativity , matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity . title: Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries
summary: On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.
body: Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth. The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa. The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe . But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us. "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker , who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview.
